newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Claims and budget rumors.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Claims and budget rumors.

text.p: Investors in U.S. Treasuries on Thursday will scrutinize second-tier data on the jobs market and entertain any new talk from Washington about negotiations on a balanced budget agreement, experts said.
The Labor Department releases first-time jobless claims at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and the Conference Board puts out its U.S. help-wanted advertising index for March at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, predicted unemployment claims for the week ended April 19 fell to 328,000 from 332,000 in the previous week.
In February, the help-wanted index jumped three points to 90.0.
If jobless claims fell to 320,000 or 315,000 and the help-wanted index stayed at 90.0 or rose to 92.0, that would be negative for bonds, said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.
This would suggest there is still significant strength in the job market and demand for workers that could lead to inflationary pressures, she said.
On Wednesday, the White House and Republicans traded jabs as the battle over a balanced budget agreement continued.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott called for action, saying it was President Bill Clinton's turn to give some ground. But White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the White House believes it has been "quite generous" in budget discussions with congressional Republicans.
Treasury market attention on Thursday will likely remain riveted on developments in Washington.

"A lot of people are wondering what's going on because stocks were up 170 (points) yesterday and the bond market rallied without any new data," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
"And the talk was that some hedge funds were buying, thinking that there's going to be a budget deal," Stiles said.
As a result, he said the Treasury market will be subject to more rumors about the budget on Thursday.
Indeed late in the session on Wednesday, Mississippi Republican Lott said he hopes an announcement can be made on the budget talks early next week after he confers with President Clinton.
U.S. Treasuries were weaker across the curve as trading wound down on Wednesday.

During Wednesday afternoon, the Treasury reported that its $12.5 billion auction of five-year notes produced a high yield of 6.745 percent, with a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.58-to-1. Non-competitive bids totaled $667 million.
Results of the auction were close to expectations, said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities.
Leahey attributed the decline in Treasuries to profit-taking rather than disappointment with the auction.
The auction has been relatively well distributed, Leahey said. "So, I don't think ... there's a sense that the Street's holding a lot more than it would like," he added.

As for U.S. central bank luminaries speaking on Thursday, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer will address a Forecasters Club luncheon at 1230 EDT/1630 GMT at the Cornell Club in New York. The Meyer engagement appears to be closed to the press.
Kansas City Fed President Thomas Hoenig will speak in Frankfurt. Hoenig's speech, which is tentatively scheduled for 1100 EDT/1500 GMT, will be covered by the press.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond closed 16/32 lower on Wednesday at 94-10/32 to yield 7.08 percent.
